newsitem.title: USA: Clinton appeals to Congress to help foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton appeals to Congress to help foreign policy.

text.p: With some of his key foreign policy goals under siege, President Bill Clinton appealed to the Republican-led Congress on Friday to approve a chemical weapons treaty and help him promote free trade.
"Now we face another moment of choice," Clinton said in a speech to the American Society of Newspaper Editors. "While we no longer face a single implacable foe, the enemy of our time is inaction."

Clinton spoke at a time when Russia is rankled at NATO plans to expand into former Soviet satellites, the Middle East peace process has stalemated and his China policy is under fire from House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and others.

The president touched on those issues only glancingly, choosing instead to urge action on two items he said are important to improving America's economic position and preventing rogue nations from developing poison gas.

The Chemical Weapons Convention, ratified by 70 of the 161 countries that signed it, has been held up in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chaired by Republican Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina. He says it would be ineffective and expose U.S. chemical companies to outside inspection.

Clinton has launched a full-scale effort to gain Senate passage of the global treaty, which bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons. He wants it approved by an April 29 deadline when the treaty takes effect.
"If we fail to do it we won't be there to enforce a treaty that we helped to write, leaving our military and our people more vulnerable to a silent and sudden killer," Clinton said.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott has said he expects the treaty to come before the full Senate for four or five days of debate in the week beginning April 21, which would leave little leeway if the April 29 deadline is to be met.
On trade, Clinton said America must maintain a position as a strong exporter and one way to do this was to increase trade with Latin America and Asia.

He called on Congress to give him so-called fast-track authority to negotiate a trade agreement to bring Chile into the North American Free Trade Agreement linking the United States, Mexico and Canada.
The authority would give Clinton the power to conclude a trade agreement with Chile that Congress could vote for or against but would not be able to slow down with amendments.

"If we don't seize these opportunities, our competitors surely will," said Clinton, citing reports that Latin American nations last year for the first time ever had more trade with Europe than the United States.
"These nations in Latin America are our friends. They're our partners," said Clinton.
In answer to questions from the editors, Clinton said he saw no prospect of changing the hardline U.S. embargo policy against Cuba as long as Cuba "murdered" Americans.
"The Castro government illegally shot down two planes and murdered Americans," he said in referring to a 1996 incident in which Cuban jets downed planes flown by Cuban-American demonstrators.

"Our policy toward Cuba today therefore is one that is dictated by Cuba, not by the United States. And until I see some indication of willingness to change it's going to be very difficult to persuade me to change our policy," he said.
